group.title: Global affairs
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A country’s full right to govern itself without control from others.
examples: The island fought to protect its {sovereignty}.
wrong: With full sovereignty, the country was ruled by a foreign power.

words.meaning: The work of managing relations between countries through talks.
examples: Careful {diplomacy} helped avoid a war.
wrong: Their diplomacy consisted of refusing to speak to any other nation.

words.meaning: An official ban on trade with a particular country.
examples: The {embargo} stopped all oil exports to the region.
wrong: The embargo encouraged more trade between the two countries.

words.meaning: A penalty, often on trade, that countries put on another country to make it change.
examples: New {sanctions} froze the regime’s foreign bank accounts.
wrong: The sanctions were a reward for the country’s good behavior.

words.meaning: Not supporting or joining any of the powerful groups of countries.
examples: Several {nonaligned} states refused to take sides in the dispute.
wrong: The nonaligned country joined both rival military blocs.

words.meaning: A formal agreement between countries to support each other.
examples: The three states formed a military {alliance}.
wrong: Countries in an alliance promise to attack each other.

words.meaning: A person sent by a government to deliver messages or hold talks.
examples: The president sent a special {envoy} to the peace talks.
wrong: The envoy stayed at home and spoke to no foreign leaders.

words.meaning: An important meeting between leaders of governments.
examples: World leaders met at a {summit} on climate change.
wrong: The summit was a private chat between two tourists.

words.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting for a time.
examples: Both sides agreed to a {ceasefire} over the holiday.
wrong: During the ceasefire, the fighting grew heavier than ever.

words.meaning: An agreement between enemies to stop fighting, often for a short time.
examples: A fragile {truce} was signed after months of war.
wrong: The truce was the moment both armies started to attack.

words.meaning: An armed fight by a group against its own government.
examples: Troops were sent to deal with the {insurgency} in the north.
wrong: The insurgency was a group that strongly supported the government.

words.meaning: A sudden, illegal seizing of a government’s power, often by the army.
examples: The general took power in a military {coup}.
wrong: The coup was a fair and peaceful election.

words.meaning: A government, especially one that rules strictly and is not elected fairly.
examples: The {regime} banned all opposition parties.
wrong: The regime was a small club for local gardeners.

words.meaning: To take control of another country’s land and make it part of your own.
examples: The empire {annexed} the neighboring province.
wrong: The country annexed the region by giving it full independence.

words.meaning: Protection a country gives to people who have fled danger in their own country.
examples: The journalist asked for {asylum} after leaving her country.
wrong: He was given asylum and sent straight back to the danger.

words.meaning: Concerned with helping people who are suffering.
examples: The agency sent {humanitarian} aid to the flood zone.
wrong: The humanitarian mission was set up to make people suffer.

words.meaning: The work of international forces sent to stop fighting in an area.
examples: The soldiers are on a {peacekeeping} mission abroad.
wrong: Peacekeeping troops were sent to start a new war.

words.meaning: Involving three or more countries.
examples: The trade deal came out of {multilateral} talks.
wrong: The multilateral talks involved only one country.

words.meaning: Involving two countries or groups.
examples: The two neighbors signed a {bilateral} trade agreement.
wrong: The bilateral meeting included twenty different countries.

words.meaning: Done by one country or group without the agreement of others.
examples: The country made a {unilateral} decision to leave the deal.
wrong: The unilateral decision was agreed by every member state.

words.meaning: Linked to how geography affects power and relations between countries.
examples: The canal has huge {geopolitical} importance.
wrong: The geopolitical issue had nothing to do with countries or power.

words.meaning: A very powerful country with great influence across the world.
examples: After the war, two {superpowers} dominated world politics.
wrong: The superpower was a tiny state with no influence at all.

words.meaning: Control or strong influence of one country or group over others.
examples: The empire’s {hegemony} lasted for two centuries.
wrong: Their hegemony meant they had no influence over anyone.

words.meaning: To help two sides who disagree to reach an agreement.
examples: Norway offered to {mediate} between the two governments.
wrong: She mediated the dispute by taking one side and fueling the anger.

words.meaning: Action by a country to get involved in another country’s problems.
examples: Many opposed military {intervention} in the region.
wrong: The intervention meant staying out of the matter completely.

words.meaning: The forcing of people to leave their homes, for example by war.
examples: The conflict caused the {displacement} of a million people.
wrong: Displacement allowed families to stay safely in their homes.

words.meaning: People from one country or group who live spread around the world.
examples: The Irish {diaspora} celebrates the festival in many cities.
wrong: A diaspora is a group who have never left their home village.

words.meaning: A policy of protecting home industries by taxing or limiting imports.
examples: Rising {protectionism} hurt global trade.
wrong: Protectionism means removing every tax on foreign goods.

words.meaning: An office in a foreign city that helps its own citizens and gives visas.
examples: I renewed my passport at the {consulate} in Chicago.
wrong: The consulate is a private hotel for tourists.

words.meaning: A group of people sent to represent a country or organization.
examples: A trade {delegation} visited the capital.
wrong: The delegation represented nobody but themselves.

words.meaning: A formal agreement between countries or groups.
examples: The peace {accord} ended years of fighting.
wrong: The accord was a bitter disagreement that ended all talks.

words.meaning: The reducing or removing of a country’s weapons.
examples: The treaty called for nuclear {disarmament}.
wrong: Disarmament means building as many weapons as possible.

words.meaning: To formally leave a country or group and become independent.
examples: The region voted to {secede} from the federation.
wrong: The state seceded by joining the union even more closely.

words.meaning: The condition of being an independent country or a state in a federation.
examples: The territory campaigned for {statehood} for decades.
wrong: After gaining statehood, the region lost all its political rights.

words.meaning: To send a suspected criminal back to the country where they are wanted for trial.
examples: The suspect was {extradited} to face fraud charges.
wrong: They extradited him by letting him stay in the country forever.

words.meaning: The legal protection that stops diplomats being arrested in a foreign country.
examples: The attaché could not be arrested because of {diplomatic immunity}.
wrong: Thanks to diplomatic immunity, the diplomat was jailed by local police.

words.meaning: A contest between countries to build more and better weapons.
examples: The two powers were locked in an {arms race}.
wrong: In an arms race, both countries destroy their weapons.

words.meaning: A situation where no country or group is strong enough to control the others.
examples: The new alliance changed the {balance of power} in Europe.
wrong: The balance of power gave one nation total control over all.

words.meaning: A final demand that comes with a threat if it is not met.
examples: They gave the government an {ultimatum}: withdraw or face sanctions.
wrong: The ultimatum was a gentle suggestion with no deadline.

words.meaning: A government’s plan for dealing with other countries.
examples: Trade is central to the country’s {foreign policy}.
wrong: Foreign policy covers only local school and road budgets.
